_comment: Clues and annotations authored for the grid in sample_fill_11.json. Keyed by entry id. Consumed by tools/build_authored_puzzle.py, which merges these with the fill geometry to produce puzzles/A001.js.

1-across.clue: Space losing its head at speed (4)

blocks.note: SPACE with its head — the leading S — taken off

annotation.walkthrough: 'Space losing its head' means drop the first letter of SPACE, which leaves PACE. That is the definition, 'speed' — the pace of a race. The surface pretends to describe an astronaut losing his nerve.

'Rebuilt' is the anagram indicator, and the fodder is NAPLES. Shuffle those six letters and you get PLANES, the 'aircraft'. The surface remembers that Naples really was rebuilt after wartime bombing — by aircraft.

8-across.clue: Tea here, or in that place (5)

blocks.note: the word itself, lifted straight from the clue

annotation.walkthrough: 'Tea' gives its abbreviation T, then 'here' supplies HERE. Run them together for T + HERE = THERE, meaning 'in that place'. Watch for words that do double duty like this: 'here' is both surface English and raw material.

'Disturbed' says to rearrange, and the fodder is DREAM. Its five letters give ARMED, which is 'carrying a gun'. A disturbed dream and an armed intruder belong to the same bad night, which is what makes the surface hang together.

annotation.definitionNote: 'The press' is a collective singular while REPORTERS is plural; setters allow the swap because the press simply is the body of reporters.

blocks.note: re = concerning, the word at the top of a memo

annotation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' is RE, as in the heading of a memo, and 'hotel staff' are PORTERS. RE + PORTERS spells REPORTERS, 'the press'. The whole clue reads like a genuine memo heading, which is exactly the disguise it wants.

blocks.note: the crossword worker is almost always an ANT, occasionally a BEE

annotation.walkthrough: 'Help' gives ASSIST and 'worker' gives ANT — one of the first pieces of crossword shorthand worth memorising. ASSIST + ANT makes ASSISTANT, a 'Deputy'. 'Will' is only a link word, joining definition to wordplay.

blocks.note: MORGAN once the M has gone

annotation.walkthrough: Take MORGAN and drop 'a million' — the letter M — and ORGAN remains. An organ is a 'Newspaper', in the sense of a party's or a union's official journal. The surface invites you to read it as a headline about a presenter losing money.

16-across.clue: Bury a bit of the sprinter (5)

annotation.walkthrough: 'A bit of' signals a hidden word, so look inside the following words: spr-INTER conceals INTER. To 'Bury' someone is to inter them. Hidden words hide best in long words you read past without pausing.

blocks.note: p = piano, the musical instruction to play softly

annotation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' is P — piano on a score — and a 'contract' is a LEASE. P + LEASE gives PLEASE, meaning to 'delight'. The surface sounds like an instruction to sign something without fuss.

blocks.note: what you do in church is pray

annotation.walkthrough: 'Heard' tells you to listen rather than read. What is done 'in church' is PRAY, and said aloud that is PREY — the definition, 'Quarry'. Quarry looks like a hole in the ground until you remember it also means hunted animal.

1-down.clue: Dwindles as time enters the Lords (6)

annotation.definitionNote: PETERS means 'dwindles' only inside the phrasal verb 'peters out', so the definition is leaning on that idiom rather than on the bare word.

blocks.note: members of the House of Lords are peers

annotation.walkthrough: 'The Lords' are PEERS, and 'time' is T. 'Enters' puts the T inside: PE-T-ERS. The answer PETERS means 'Dwindles' — as in a supply that peters out. The surface pictures a clock running in the upper chamber.

blocks.note: c = cold, as marked on a tap

annotation.walkthrough: 'Cold' is C, the letter on the tap, and 'heap' supplies HEAP. C + HEAP gives CHEAP, 'inexpensive'. A cold heap is also a fair description of a car worth very little, which is the joke in the surface.
'Chief' gives LEADER and 'vessel' gives SHIP; run them together for LEADERSHIP, which is 'direction' in the sense of guidance. The surface describes a flagship, and 'provides' is only a link word.

blocks.note: to name a thing is to call it something

annotation.walkthrough: Two definitions and nothing else. To 'call' something is to NAME it, and 'celebrities' are NAMES — as in a party full of big names. Two words is about as short as a fair cryptic clue gets.

blocks.note: ID = identity, as on a card

annotation.walkthrough: 'Identity' is ID and 'southeast' is SE. 'Tucked into' puts the ID inside SE: S-ID-E. A SIDE is a 'flank'. The surface reads like a note about hiding a passport.

blocks.note: re is the second note of the scale — doh, re, mi

annotation.walkthrough: 'A note' is RE from the tonic sol-fa, and 'gifts' are PRESENTS. RE + PRESENTS spells REPRESENTS, meaning 'Depicts'. Beware 'note': it can be RE, TE, DO, N for the musical scale or a banknote, or even a letter.

11-down.clue: Oyster served on the ground floor (6)

blocks.note: surface only — it makes the clue read as a restaurant order

annotation.walkthrough: 'Ground' is the anagram indicator: grind up the letters of OYSTER and they resettle as STOREY, a 'floor' of a building. The trick is that 'ground floor' reads as one phrase, so the indicator hides inside the definition's own scenery.

blocks.note: an auger is a boring tool; five letters to rearrange

annotation.walkthrough: 'Twisted' calls for an anagram of 'auger', the drill bit — and a twisted auger is a nicely literal picture. Its letters give ARGUE, which is to 'Row', the verb that rhymes with cow.
'Rewritten' is the anagram indicator and LATER is the fodder. Rearranged, those letters give ALTER, meaning to 'change'. The surface sounds like an editor's margin note, which is the point.

blocks.note: read backwards it becomes the answer

annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned' says to reverse, and POOL turned round is LOOP — a 'circuit'. In a down clue a reversal reads upwards, so the P that started the word ends it.
